original_question: For a geometric sequence (q^n)_{n in N} with q in (1/2, 1), does there always exist a subsequence (q^{n_k})_{k in N} whose achievement set E(q^{n_k}) is a Cantorval?
target_in_paper: Section 1 ("The Kakeya conditions"), Problem 6: the geometric-sequence specialization of the thinning-out question posed immediately after Problem 5. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2512.17285))
correct_elements: Your draft already identifies the exact official open problem almost verbatim: it asks whether every geometric sequence $(q^n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ with $q\in(1/2,1)$ has a subsequence whose achievement set is a Cantorval. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2512.17285))
missing_details: Define the notation for the achievement set: for a real sequence $y=(y_k)$, $E(y):=\{\sum_{k\in A} y_k : A\subseteq \mathbb{N}\}\subseteq \mathbb{R}$. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2512.17285))
Clarify that $(q^{n_k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$ is a genuine subsequence, i.e. the indices satisfy $n_1<n_2<\cdots$ in $\mathbb{N}$.
Make the ambient setting explicit: the paper is working with real sequences and real subsums. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2512.17285))

If the question is to be fully stand-alone, define "Cantorval" in the paper’s sense: a compact set $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ such that the endpoints of every $A$-gap are accumulation points both of other $A$-gaps and of $A$-intervals. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2512.17285))

To mirror the nearby context faithfully, note that Problem 6 is presented as the geometric special case of Problem 5, which asks the same thinning-out question under the hypothesis $r_n>x_n$ for all $n$, where $r_n:=\sum_{i>n}x_i$. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2512.17285))
refined_question:
For every real number $q\in(1/2,1)$, does the geometric sequence $(q^n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ contain a subsequence $(q^{n_k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$, with $n_1<n_2<\cdots$, such that its achievement set
$E\big((q^{n_k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\big):=\left\{\sum_{k\in A} q^{n_k}: A\subseteq\mathbb{N}\right\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}$
is a Cantorval?
justification: The nearest official formulation is exactly Problem 6, not the broader Problem 5 and not the earlier Jones problems. The paper first defines achievement sets, Cantorvals, and the remainder/Kakeya notation, then discusses thinning out slowly convergent series and immediately states the broad subsequence problem (Problem 5) followed by its geometric-sequence specialization (Problem 6). Your draft already captures that official specialization; the only real gaps are the definitions needed to make the question fully stand-alone. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2512.17285))
